title: Surveying
summary: Learn the basics of land surveying: types of survey and key principles, distances, scales and slope corrections, levelling and reduced levels, bearings, coordinates and areas, total stations, GNSS, drones and GIS, and setting out and land tenure. All calculations were checked in code.
audience: School leavers, construction and mapping workers, and students considering surveying or geomatics

body.p: Surveying measures the positions of points on, above or below the Earth's surface, and uses those measurements to produce maps, plans and boundaries and to set out construction. Almost every road, building, pipeline, mine and land title begins with a survey.

list: Cadastral (land) surveys define property boundaries for land registration and title deeds.
Topographic surveys map the shape of the land, features and heights.
Engineering surveys set out roads, buildings, bridges and pipelines and check construction.
Mining and hydrographic surveys measure mines and the beds of seas, lakes and rivers.
Geodetic surveys cover large areas, accounting for the Earth's curvature, and provide the control network that other surveys tie into.

body.p: Work from the whole to the part: establish accurate control points first, then fill in detail, so errors do not build up. Always include checks, such as closing a traverse back on a known point, to detect mistakes.

body.tip: Secure land titles depend on accurate cadastral surveys; in many countries only a registered land surveyor may sign them.

body.p: Distances are measured with tapes, electronic distance measurement (EDM) in total stations, or satellite positioning. Plans always show horizontal distances, so slope measurements must be reduced.
Horizontal distance = slope distance x cos(angle of slope). A 100 m slope distance at 10° gives 100 x cos 10° = 98.48 m horizontally. Ignoring this on hilly ground causes boundary and area errors.

list: A scale of 1 : 500 means 1 cm on the plan represents 500 cm (5 m) on the ground. So 4 cm on the plan is 4 x 500 = 2000 cm, or 20 m.
Going the other way at 1 : 2000, a 50 m distance is 50 / 2000 m = 25 mm on the plan.
Large scales (1 : 100 to 1 : 500) show detail for buildings; small scales (1 : 50 000) cover regions.
Always draw a scale bar, because printed plans can be enlarged or reduced.

body.tip: Tapes stretch, sag and change with temperature; good practice applies corrections and measures each line twice.

body.p: Levelling finds height differences using a level (an instrument with a horizontal line of sight) and a graduated staff. Heights are given as reduced levels (RL) relative to a datum, such as mean sea level or a site benchmark.

From a benchmark of RL 100.00 m, a backsight (BS) of 1.50 m and a foresight (FS) of 0.80 m to the next point show a rise of 1.50 - 0.80 = 0.70 m, so its RL is 100.70 m. Moving on, a backsight of 1.20 m and a foresight of 2.10 m on that point and the next give a fall of 0.90 m, so the RL is 99.80 m.

list: A smaller staff reading means higher ground.
Check: the sum of backsights minus the sum of foresights equals the last RL minus the first RL.
Close the levelling back on the starting benchmark or another known one to measure the misclosure.

body.p: Levels are used to set floor levels, drainage falls, road gradients and earthworks volumes.

body.tip: Keep backsight and foresight distances roughly equal to cancel instrument errors.

body.p: Directions are measured as bearings, clockwise from north, from 0° to 360°. The back bearing is the bearing plus or minus 180°: a line on a bearing of 45° has a back bearing of 225°; a bearing of 300° has a back bearing of 120°.

Surveyors give points coordinates: an easting (E) and northing (N). From point A to point B with a change of 40 m east and 30 m north, the distance is √(40² + 30²) = 50 m. The bearing is the angle from north: arctan(40 / 30), about 53.13°.

The coordinate (shoelace) method finds the area of any shape from its corner coordinates. A rectangle with corners (0, 0), (40, 0), (40, 30) and (0, 30) gives 1200 m². A triangle at (0, 0), (60, 0) and (20, 40) also gives 1200 m²: ½ x base 60 x height 40. Area in hectares divides by 10 000, so 1200 m² is 0.12 ha.

body.tip: Theodolites and total stations measure angles; always observe on both faces of the instrument and take the mean.

lessons.title: Total stations, GNSS, drones and GIS

body.p: Surveying technology has changed rapidly. Instruments that once needed teams of people and days of calculation now record and compute positions instantly, and data flows straight into design and mapping software.

list: Total stations combine an electronic theodolite and EDM, recording angles and distances and computing coordinates.

GNSS (satellite positioning such as GPS) gives positions anywhere with a clear view of the sky. Handheld units are accurate to a few metres; survey-grade RTK GNSS, using a base station or correction network, achieves centimetre accuracy.
Drones with cameras produce detailed maps (orthophotos) and 3D surface models through photogrammetry, quickly covering farms, mines and informal settlements.
Laser scanning (LiDAR) captures millions of points to model buildings and terrain.
Geographic Information Systems (GIS) store, analyse and map spatial data, such as land parcels, roads, services and flood zones.

body.p: Modern tools are fast, but the principles of control, checks and careful records still apply. Data must be tied to the national coordinate system and datum so that surveys fit together.

body.tip: Learn free GIS software such as QGIS; it is widely used in African government and NGO work.

lessons.title: Setting out, land tenure and careers

body.p: Setting out transfers a design from drawings onto the ground: marking building corners, road centrelines and levels with pegs and profiles. Checking diagonals confirms rectangles are square; the 3-4-5 triangle gives a quick right angle.

Secure land rights encourage investment and reduce conflict. Many countries combine formal title deeds with customary tenure. Low-cost, fit-for-purpose land administration, using drones, satellite images and community mapping, is helping record land rights faster and more cheaply, including women's rights to land.

Paths include diplomas for survey technicians and degrees in surveying or geomatics, followed by professional registration. Surveyors work in land offices, construction, mining, utilities, mapping agencies and private practice. Ethics matter: boundary surveys affect people's homes and livelihoods.

body.tip: Never move or remove a survey beacon; in most countries it is an offence, and it can cause long boundary disputes.
